strengths: Addresses important gap in domain-specific, implicit harmful prompt generation—a timely and underexplored problem for LLM safety

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: tests across 6 LLM families, includes safety fine-tuning experiments (Table 3) demonstrating practical utility, cross-domain analysis, ablation studies, and model-agnostic evaluation
Strong practical validation: Table 3 shows models fine-tuned on RiskAtlas achieve 12% ASR against RA-Implicit✓ vs. 55-66% for public datasets, while maintaining MMLU capability preservation
Systematic and well-designed pipeline with appropriate filtering mechanisms (harmfulness, fluency, semantic preservation, obfuscation success) and reasonable design choices
Good reproducibility: detailed parameter settings, SPARQL queries, abstracted prompt templates provided, and code/datasets promised for release
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem, comprehensive methodology, and informative figures and tables
Responsible ethical framework clarifying defensive research purpose and providing abstracted rather than directly usable attacks
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: excludes TRIDENT (most relevant related work), no comparison with other semi-automated approaches, weakening assessment of contribution relative to existing methods

Indirect evaluation of core claims: obfuscation success relies on target model behavior (circular evaluation using same model family for generation and evaluation), and large gap between RA-Implicit (61.58% ASR) and RA-Implicit✓ (84.92% ASR) suggests inconsistent filtering
Missing critical specification: 'quality model M_qual' for semantic preservation and fluency is not defined, affecting reproducibility and understanding of quality thresholds
Implicit/explicit distinction lacks validation: no human evaluation to verify prompts are truly implicit or realistic; some examples (Appendix E) still appear fairly direct
LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation has known consistency issues; using proprietary models (Gemini, Claude, GPT) as judges may introduce biases; no inter-rater reliability analysis beyond 2-of-3 agreement
Limited scope of obfuscation evaluation: OSR measured only on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct; transfer of obfuscated prompts to other models not explored
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: why is medicine OSR so low (29.03%)? What harm categories are harder to obfuscate? Limited discussion despite significant variance
Relatively small dataset (200 prompts per dataset, 50 per domain) with no analysis of dataset size impact on downstream safety improvements
Incremental novelty: combines existing techniques (KG-guided generation, obfuscation rewriting) without fundamental innovation

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap in LLM safety research: domain-specific implicit harmful prompts are more realistic than existing explicit-only datasets
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 6 models and 4 domains with strong, consistent results (RiskAtlas-Implicit✓ achieves 84.92% ASR vs. 23.92% for public datasets)
Coherent end-to-end framework combining knowledge-graph-guided generation with dual-path obfuscation rewriting

Excellent experimental rigor with multiple evaluation settings, ablation studies (Table 7), cross-domain analysis (Table 5-6), and safety fine-tuning experiments demonstrating practical utility (Table 3)
Strong reproducibility commitments: detailed appendices with SPARQL queries, hyperparameters, prompt templates, and promise of code/dataset release
Well-written paper with clear motivation, methodology, and effective use of concrete examples (Figure 2, Appendix E)
Safety fine-tuning results show tangible benefits: RA-Implicit alignment reduces ASR from 36-66% (public datasets) to 6-12% on RA-Implicit✓ attacks
weaknesses: Evaluation of obfuscation success relies on subjective LLM-as-a-Judge assessment (3 judges, majority voting) without human validation to confirm that implicit prompts are actually more realistic—only proxy metrics provided (PPL, cosine similarity)
Limited technical novelty: KG extraction from Wikidata is straightforward; obfuscation builds directly on prior work (DrAttack, MIST); dual-path shows modest improvements (~3% at κ=30)
Baseline comparisons incomplete: TRIDENT (most relevant domain-specific safety work) excluded; comparison fairness with public datasets unclear due to different distributions

Dataset filtering concerns: only 2 prompts per entity-category pair; harmfulness threshold of 0.9 is very restrictive; no analysis of whether this introduces systematic bias or leaves important entities underrepresented

Scope limitations: only 4 English-language domains; generalization to other high-risk domains (aviation, energy, infrastructure) unclear; single KG source (Wikidata); acknowledged reliance on relation-based rather than recursive queries
Algorithm 1 underspecified: path initialization, state management, and fallback mechanism lack clarity; why alternating paths yield improvement is not analyzed
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-rater agreement (kappa) for 3-judge evaluation, or analysis of variance across runs
No error analysis (which prompt types fail to obfuscate?), transfer analysis (cross-model generalization?), or computational cost discussion
Knowledge graph construction choices (thresholds in Table 9) appear arbitrary; Wikipedia sitelinks as popularity signal is crude; no sensitivity analysis
Evaluation relies on proprietary models (Gemini, GPT-5 Mini, Claude) for ASR assessment, limiting reproducibility

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing gap between explicit and implicit domain-specific harmful prompts
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 model families, multiple benchmarks, and defense mechanisms (LlamaGuard, SemanticSmooth)
Strong empirical results: SG-Implicit achieves 61.58% ASR vs. 5-24% for baselines while maintaining acceptable fluency (PPL ~80)
Thorough reproducibility support: fixed seeds, detailed parameters, three-judge ensembles, code/dataset release promised
Systematic two-stage pipeline effectively combining knowledge graph grounding with obfuscation rewriting
Extensive ablations and cross-domain analysis demonstrating consistency across medicine, finance, law, education
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (KG-based grounding, prompt obfuscation) without fundamental innovation; two-strategy approach gains only ~3% over single-strategy (Table 7)
Heavy reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge without validation: no human evaluation, inter-judge agreement, or false-positive analysis; ASR definition is subjective
Core claims under-supported: 'implicit prompts are more realistic' and 'better reflect real-world threats' lack evidence from user studies or threat modeling
Knowledge graph construction appears ad-hoc: root selection and sitelink thresholds (T=25-80) lack systematic justification; impact on coverage/quality unquantified
Unfair baseline comparisons: public benchmarks (AdvBench, Do-Not-Answer) not optimized for domain-specific or implicit attacks; limited direct comparison with TRIDENT
Weak generalization evidence: only 4 conservative domains; unclear if approach scales to higher-risk domains; no ablation comparing domain-specific vs. generic implicit prompts
Statistical rigor absent: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or bootstrap analysis; small samples (50 prompts/domain) and point estimates only
Missing critical validations: semantic preservation relies on embeddings not validated for domain-specific shifts; quality model (Mqual) not validated; fine-tuning uses only 200 pairs
Computational cost under-analyzed: StealthGraph uses 2-4× more tokens than baselines (Table 10); 'manageable' claim insufficiently supported
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: OSR varies 29-43% across domains (Table 5) without investigation; why is medicine harder to obfuscate?

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gap in LLM safety: most benchmarks focus on explicit attacks that modern defenses readily detect, while implicit domain-specific prompts represent more realistic threats
Novel two-strategy obfuscation approach thoughtfully combining direct and context-card enhanced rewriting with clear motivation

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: multiple model families, LLM-as-judge with 3-model ensemble, defense-oriented evaluation (LlamaGuard, SemanticSmooth), and alternative assessment frameworks demonstrating robustness
Strong cross-domain analysis revealing meaningful domain-specific harm patterns and showing systematic improvements over public benchmarks (SG-Implicit✓ 84.92% vs 5.17-23.92%)
Thorough ablation studies validating core design choices and clear reproduction details including SPARQL queries, parameter tables, and promised code/data release
Practical framework with demonstrated benefits for safety fine-tuning—models aligned on StealthGraph variants show greater robustness to implicit attacks than those aligned on public datasets
weaknesses: Modest obfuscation success rates (29-43% OSR across domains) mean majority of generated prompts fail obfuscation, undermining practical utility and suggesting the two-strategy approach incompletely solves the stated problem

Evaluation of obfuscation success uses only Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as target model with unclear transferability to other models, contradicting the claim of creating 'reusable datasets'; high cross-model variance in ASR (87.5-91%) suggests strong model-specificity
Lacks human evaluation of stealthiness—no evidence that implicit prompts actually feel more natural or would survive human inspection; perplexity (79.87) is imperfect proxy and still relatively high
Knowledge graph construction relies on ad-hoc design choices (popularity filtering, root nodes, thresholds) without systematic analysis of how these affect downstream results or entity coverage

Limited component-level novelty: KG-guided generation straightforwardly applies existing ideas, obfuscation rewriting heavily builds on prior work (DrAttack, MIST); main novelty is in combination rather than fundamental methodological innovation

Computational cost significantly higher than baselines (17,500 vs 4,367-14,246 tokens/target) with missing wall-clock time analysis; SG-Origin explicit prompts fail to clearly outperform other explicit benchmarks suggesting limited KG-guidance advantage

Algorithm 1 fallback mechanism to original prompt could introduce bias; insufficient implementation details for quality model Mqual; missing analysis of failure modes and what domain knowledge types are most useful for harm generation
